stem.text: An ester of structural formula CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
What are the two organic products of this reaction?

explanation.text: In CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> the acid part is CH<sub>3</sub>CO– (ethanoate, two carbons, including the C=O carbon) and the alcohol part is –OCH<sub>3</sub> (from methanol). The ester is methyl ethanoate.

Alkaline hydrolysis gives the salt of the acid, not the free acid, because the carboxylic acid formed is neutralised by the excess NaOH: CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + NaOH → CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na + CH<sub>3</sub>OH.

optionAnalysis.text: These are the products of acid hydrolysis. With aqueous NaOH the ethanoic acid is converted to sodium ethanoate.
Splits the ester the wrong way round and gives the free acid; the CH<sub>3</sub> next to C=O belongs to the acid part.
Methyl ethanoate + NaOH gives sodium ethanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>Na) and methanol (CH<sub>3</sub>OH).
Correctly gives a sodium salt, but splits the ester the wrong way round: it would be the products of ethyl methanoate, HCO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.

reasoningChain: CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>: CH<sub>3</sub>CO– from ethanoic acid, –OCH<sub>3</sub> from methanol.
Alkaline hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt plus the alcohol.
Products: sodium ethanoate and methanol, option C.

inferredMistakes.text: Giving the acid hydrolysis products (ethanoic acid) when the conditions are alkaline.
Reading the ester name from the formula in the wrong order and swapping the acid and alcohol parts.
